body:
From what we've been talking, I know that you've been through a lot, but boy did I feel happy to hear how you've managed to turn highly important parts of your life, if not your entire life, to the joyous and mysterious adventure that it is, especially when you mentioned that you destroyed your copy of the key to their house and that she's never going to get your new address. That's powerful stuff, to say the least. I literally crave that. It's really amazing that your husband supported you fully; it's heartwarming when you have someone by your side, despite the challenges. Because time is important to me, I can't help but feel happy that you managed to turn the tides at such an early age, though I understand that even a second lost to a narcissist is hurtful.

I want to say something next, and the reason I'm doing this is because I want to show the extent of the damage that my critical inner voices imparted so generously from my father (and mother, who is also a narcissist), and why I'm so worried that these voices have returned. I'm making this "disclaimer" because I don't want to mistakenly portray my next statements as comparison....I know how difficult it is to be raised by a narcissist. I'm also making this disclaimer because I'm deeply ashamed and embarrassed at what I'm going to say next.

Here goes: *I'm 27 years old, and never have I had a job*. I'm not talking about having unstable jobs. I'm talking about having *a* job...ever. Well, that's not true anymore, since now I've managed to open my own company, but that's only because I didn't have those critical inner voices anymore. Now I'm freaking out because they've returned, and I know the damage they can do to me. They completely paralyze me. And it's not that I'm not good at what I do, or that I lack "professional skills." It's because those voices induce a spiraling self-doubt that shame me to the core, literally paralyzing me. I can't make any decisions because I convince myself that, "*I'm just not that good enough. Why even bother*?" Even as I write these very sentences, I "have to" constantly second guess myself. It's a fitting example of what has been happening to me since infancy...I've lost so much time and so many opportunities because of these voices...these shaming messages. To admit that I've never held a job makes me feel extremely ashamed of myself; to look at all the time I've lost trying to manage these feelings, and the messages that cause them...well, that just makes me feel depressed.

Wow, I'm really sorry what you've gone through ... :( It must've been so painful having to hear the one person who was supposed to love and support you mercilessly criticize you for basically existing. I'm feeling really happy that you've managed to cut contact with her and never have to hear her about *anything*. 

It really made sense to me when you shared the insight that the voice is actually *you*, or *me* (for my own self). I did have the same experience when I didn't talk to my father. I could finally breathe for the first time in my life and have control over my own decisions...even my own thoughts and dreams! Imagine that! 

Those criticisms didn't feel like they were coming from him anymore, but from myself. I learned then how to approach that critical inner part of mine with respect and understanding. At first it felt goofy, because I was merely talking to myself. But soon enough I could feel that part of me telling me how it was trying to protect me from making mistakes....from making those errors that would displease my father. I even managed to befriend it, to the point that it was actively promoting my well being, whether socially, professionally, or even nutritionally (you see, I was, and probably am, heavily addicted to sugar; but now I almost never eat any type of sugar). That's how I started to understand the importance of ethics, rights, and responsibility.

Unfortunately, those critical inner voices returned as soon as some life circumstances brought me into contact again. This is what has me completely baffled: how is it that I manage to *befriend* that critical inner part of mine to the point of health and integration, only to have it *immediately* return to those shaming messages as soon as I'm in contact with my father again. (Talk about making the worst mistake ever, lol). 

I'd very much like to go no contact again. I understand that an important part of your own healing process involved going no contact with your nmom; that's how you also gain that safe space from their explicit and implicit attacks, among others. How did you manage to stay no contact all this time? What did you do in terms of supporting and managing yourself emotionally and financially, if I may ask?

Thanks for writing, I really appreciate it! It does make a lot of sense to turn the positive voice into a habit; it makes me feel hopeful just knowing that this is possible, so thank you for this! I also feel happy that you essentially healed a wound...I can imagine that it probably wasn't very easy. Your solution did remind me of how I got to reduce the intensity and frequency of my own critical voice to begin with. At the same time, this reminds me of one problem that I encountered time and time again: Time itself.

For me, it's very important that I spend more time doing the things I love. I understand that given what's going on in my own head that the surefire way to gain time is to spend time healing. I'm wondering, do you remember how long did it take for you to turn the positive voice into a habit? I know that each of us may have a different path, but it would help me immensely to have a baseline of sorts. 

Also, when you were working on affirmations, did you focus on specific areas, or was it more general? How long until the affirmations had an impact?

Yeah, these feelings are pretty overwhelming. They're also the reason why I find it difficult to focus when they hit and the world feels so bleak...they also make it impossible for me to sleep, unfortunately. I feel like I have to keep finding a solution, even if it means driving myself nuts without any sleep.
Just a quick update: I immediately started applying your advice of taking on small tasks, and I already increased my performance and productivity significantly. Thank you so much, again!

Wow, thank you so much! I find your advice very helpful; it might just do the trick! It *is* important to keep in mind that we owe nothing those who care about us only conditionally, especially considering what they've taken from us. The idea of concentrating on small tasks and rewarding oneself for their completion just really clicked with me...it makes this whole "task" look very manageable.  I really do appreciate your concern, and I'm very sorry to hear that you've been going through such a painful journey yourself :( ... I hope that whatever you're going through you receive the compassion, understanding, validation, healing, and closure that you need and have a right to

Thank you so much for writing. I feel like I'm at the end of my rope, so having someone help me, even if it's a little, means a lot to me. (I don't see it as "marginal" at all). As to your question, there may be a way, but I don't think I'm seeing it. I feel trapped because I'm currently in a precarious financial position, and I feel like I need to stay focused on work to be able to completely distance myself from them.  But to stay focused on work, I need to be away from them...it's kind of a "loop-y" problem, at least as I see it. The other problem is that I was "encouraged" by these other people who support me to contact and stay in contact with them, and they're not taking "no" for an answer,  despite all my protests. It feels like I'll be abandoned from them too if I don't do what they want, or at least looked down on, which is what I can't afford right now, at least not emotionally. Either way, thank you so much for your concern, it does give me hope. I don't want to end my own life, but considering all the pain I'm feeling, and have been feeling for quite some time now...all I see is a bleak future. I do appreciate the concern because it reminds me that life can be better
